author: "Yannick Loth"

A blood test for ME/CFS has been reported in the press. The numbers quoted are striking: **92% sensitivity, 98% specificity, 96% accuracy.** If you have ME/CFS, a test like that sounds like the thing you have waited years for.

This post is about the comparison behind that figure — and about a sentence in our own document that we had to fix.

## What the test measures

The platform reads **3D chromosome architecture**: how DNA folds into loops inside the cell nucleus. That is a genuine epigenetic layer, different from DNA sequence and different from the methylation marks measured by standard arrays. It is a real measurement with a real biological basis — which is exactly why it deserves a careful look rather than either dismissal or enthusiasm.

The study profiled blood from **47 severely affected (housebound) ME/CFS patients and 61 healthy controls.** A 200-marker panel separated the two groups. Pathway analysis pointed at IL-2 signalling and JAK-STAT.

## The number that needs a sentence of context

"98% specificity" means: of the healthy controls, 98% were correctly identified as not having ME/CFS.

That is the whole claim. It is measured **against healthy people only.**

It is *not* a claim that the test separates ME/CFS from other fatiguing illnesses. The panel has never been tested against fibromyalgia, depression, or long-COVID fatigue. And that is the actual clinical question, because those are the conditions a real patient is usually being distinguished from.

## Our own correction

Our document previously described the 92%/98%/96% figures as coming from the **discovery cohort**. That was wrong, and we caught it while re-checking the source.

The figures come from the study's own **internal (retrospective) validation cohort** — a held-out split of the same samples. That is a meaningful distinction. It is also not an external cohort.

We have corrected the wording in three places. The distinction matters for the same reason the series exists: a number that sounds stronger than it is will be repeated as if it were stronger than it is.

## New evidence, published this year

Two things have appeared since the original paper — neither of them replication.

**A published critique.** A letter in the same journal challenges the study on ten grounds. Two of them go beyond what we say below, and appear well-founded: the cohort is described as "severe/housebound" without naming the diagnostic criteria used, so the sample cannot be reproduced from the paper; and the study's comparison to rituximab-responsive conditions is misleading, because the rituximab trial in ME/CFS was null. Several of the letter's other objections overlap points we make further down — an ambiguous control group, and the absence of external validation — and one is worth adding: the study did not adjust for medication, prior infection, or smoking differences between the groups. The original authors have not replied.

The critique has its own interest. Its authors promote oxygen-ozone therapy for ME/CFS, and their demand that the paper cite their own earlier work is the least persuasive of its points. The letter's citation claim does hold up: the study cites cytokine and natural-killer-cell work, but not the 1990s studies the letter has in mind. We cite the critique as a critique, not as proof that the test is invalid.

**A cross-condition methylation study.** A single, not-yet-replicated study of 188 women, run independently of the platform vendor, compared ME/CFS with **fibromyalgia** directly — the comparison the EpiSwitch panel never made. It found two separate methylation axes:

- one axis separated ME/CFS from **both** fibromyalgia and controls, and tracked post-exertional malaise and cognitive symptoms;
- a second axis separated **both** patient groups from controls but **not** from each other, and tracked broad symptom burden.

The second of those axes is the one that matters here: it tracks general illness burden rather than the diagnosis.

And because the EpiSwitch classifier was trained against healthy controls only, we **cannot rule out** that a portion of its signal is the same kind of burden component.

One caveat belongs on that sentence. The burden axis was found in **methylation**; EpiSwitch measures **3D architecture**. Those are different molecular layers, so this is an analogy and a warning — not a measurement of the EpiSwitch panel.

## What this means for patients

- The test is **research-stage**. It is not a validated clinical diagnostic.
- The figure you may have seen was measured against healthy people. It has not been shown to distinguish ME/CFS from fibromyalgia, depression, or long COVID.
- The study is a single analysis by the company that makes the platform. The paper's competing-interest statement lists its authors as full-time Oxford BioDynamics employees, and the company funded the work. There is no independent replication.
- The pathway it reports is plausible, and independent T-cell work links 3D chromatin topology to IL-2/JAK-STAT signalling — though not in ME/CFS. The *classifier* is the unproven part.

You may find this test offered for sale. **Availability is not validation.** A test can be marketed while its specificity question is still open, and we cannot recommend paying for it to make a clinical decision.

The next step is an independent cohort, run by a group with no stake in the platform, that tests ME/CFS against other fatiguing illnesses.

Meanwhile, nothing here changes what you should do today. The approaches the paper can support — pacing inside an energy envelope, and treating symptoms individually — do not depend on this test existing.

*The thread of this series: a document that cannot show its errors cannot be trusted with its conclusions. We found one of ours — a figure described as coming from the wrong cohort — and corrected it.*
